headline: A scalp drug
heads to FDA.
dek: Cosmo reports a year of results for clascoterone solution and plans a US filing in early 2027.
photoAlt: A man with a thinning crown holds a stapled report.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Nov 2, 2026 · Clinical review pending

glance.label: Approved only for acne
glance.line: Clascoterone is FDA approved as Winlevi 1% cream for acne. The 5% hair solution is not approved.

glance.label: 1,465 men, two trials
glance.line: SCALP1 and SCALP2: six months against an inactive solution, then six more for responders.

glance.label: Filing planned
glance.line: Cosmo says a US filing is planned for early 2027. No results are published yet.

body: On April 15, 2026, Cosmo Pharmaceuticals, a company based in Dublin, Ireland, announced a year of results for an experimental scalp solution for male pattern hair loss.[^cosmo12] The drug is clascoterone 5% solution. Cosmo said men who kept using it kept gaining hair through month 12, and that it plans to file for FDA approval: “A U.S. FDA filing is currently planned for early 2027.”[^cosmo12] It would be a different kind of hair-loss medicine. Cosmo says the solution “is designed to locally inhibit androgen receptor signalling in the scalp,”[^cosmo12] blocking the hormone signal at the follicle rather than lowering a hormone in the body.

The molecule itself is not new. FDA approved [[/clascoterone|clascoterone]] on August 26, 2020, as Winlevi, a 1% cream.[^winapp] Its label reads: “WINLEVI (clascoterone) cream is an androgen receptor inhibitor indicated for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris in patients 12 years of age and older.”[^winlevi] Even for acne, the label says “the mechanism of action of WINLEVI cream for the topical treatment of acne vulgaris is unknown.”[^winlevi] Hair loss is not an approved use. The 5% solution is still investigational, and putting the acne cream on the scalp would be off-label.

Cosmo says the hair product uses “the same active ingredient used in Winlevi”[^cosmo12] at a higher strength. The two hair-loss trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with Cassiopea SpA as the sponsor.[^scalp1][^scalp2] They are called SCALP1 and SCALP2, and were built identically.

Each enrolled men aged 18 and older with mild to moderate hair loss at the temples and the crown, rated III vertex to V on the Norwood-Hamilton scale.[^scalp1] Men applied 1.5 ml of the solution, or an identical inactive solution called a vehicle, to the balding areas twice a day.[^scalp1] Part 1 was six months, randomized and double-blind. In Part 2, men who had responded in Part 1 were randomized again, to the drug or the vehicle, for six more months in a single-blind design.[^scalp1] The main measures, at month 6, were the change in the count of non-vellus (thicker, visible) hairs in a target area of the scalp, and each man’s own rating of his hair coverage.[^scalp1] SCALP1 enrolled 703 men and finished in January 2026; SCALP2 enrolled 762 and finished in July 2025.[^scalp1][^scalp2] Cosmo says the program ran at 51 centers in the United States and Europe.[^cosmo12]

Cosmo released the six-month results in early December 2025.[^gendec] As GEN reported them, the two trials together showed a 252% relative improvement in target-area hair count with clascoterone over vehicle; SCALP2 showed 539%, and SCALP1 showed 168%.[^gendec] These are relative figures; the reports this story could open give no underlying hair counts. Side effects that began during treatment were reported in 5.1% of men on clascoterone and 6.1% on vehicle, according to Cosmo’s figures as reported by GEN.[^gendec] On the gap between the two trials, Diana Harbort, president of Cosmo’s dermatology division, told GEN: “It’s not uncommon for a Phase III program with two identical studies to have a bit of variability in results, but these both were statistically significant.”[^gendec]

The April results come from Part 2. Cosmo said men who stayed on clascoterone for 12 months had a “statistically significant 2.39x improvement in Target Area Hair Count (TAHC)”[^cosmo12] compared with men who had six months of the drug and were then switched to vehicle. It said the men who switched “experienced a measurable and meaningful decline in hair count.”[^cosmo12] Men on the drug for the full year also reported 24.5% higher treatment satisfaction than the vehicle groups, Cosmo said.[^cosmo12] On safety, the company said that across 12 months the drug had a profile “comparable to vehicle, with no significant systemic hormonal side effects observed.”[^cosmo12] Cosmo’s chief executive, Giovanni Di Napoli, told GEN that the six- and 12-month figures were not directly comparable, because they compare different groups of men.[^genapr]

Two hair-loss drugs are already approved. [[/finasteride|Finasteride]], approved as Propecia in December 1997,[^propapp] is a pill: “PROPECIA is a 5α-reductase inhibitor indicated for the treatment of male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) in MEN ONLY.”[^propecia] It blocks the body’s conversion of testosterone to a stronger hormone, DHT,[^propecia] and its label lists the most common side effects as “decreased libido, erectile dysfunction and ejaculation disorder.”[^propecia] [[/minoxidil|Minoxidil]] 5% is sold over the counter, and its label states its use plainly: to “regrow hair on the top of the scalp.”[^rogaine] Clascoterone would sit beside them as a third route: a liquid on the scalp aimed at the hormone receptor itself. Cosmo calls it potentially “the first novel mechanism of action introduced for male AGA in more than 30 years.”[^cosmo12]

Much is still unknown. No results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov for either trial, and no peer-reviewed paper has appeared; Cosmo says it plans to submit the full dataset to a medical journal.[^scalp1][^scalp2][^cosmo12] Until then, outside experts cannot check the hair counts, how many men responded in Part 1, or why one trial’s result was more than three times the other’s. The 12-month comparison includes only men who had already responded, so it says nothing about the men who did not.[^cosmo12] Neither trial tested clascoterone against finasteride or minoxidil.[^scalp1][^scalp2]

The safety data so far come from the 1% cream and from Cosmo’s unpublished figures. The Winlevi cream label warns that clascoterone can suppress the body’s adrenal hormone system, known as the HPA axis, and that “elevated potassium levels were observed in some subjects during the clinical trials.”[^winlevi] Those findings come from a 1% cream; the hair product is five times stronger and is meant for long-term use on the scalp. Cosmo says it found no significant hormonal side effects over a year,[^cosmo12] but those safety data have not been published.

What comes next is the filing. Cosmo says it is preparing a New Drug Application for FDA and a marketing application in Europe, with the US filing planned for early 2027.[^cosmo12] FDA would then review the full data. Until the agency acts, no clascoterone product is approved for hair loss, and the only approved clascoterone medicine remains an acne cream.[^winlevi]
